• Q: What is the largest number of points on the plain, each two of which have the equal $\ell_1$ distance?
    • If $x \in B(y)$, then $B(x) \cap B(y) \leq 2$. Where $B()$ is the $\ell_1$ ball of the plane.
      • If $x,\ y$ have \ell 1 distance $d$, what is the number of other points having the equal distance from $x$ and $y$?
      • The answer is $2$, as the inequality above asserts.
    • So, the maximal number of pairwise $\ell_1$-equidistant points on $\mathbb R^2$ is $\boxed 4$.

entry.content:
Estimation of Summations

$\frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{k=1} n^{1/k}$

By plotting, you can find that the $\frac{1}{n} \sum^\infty_{k=1} k^{1/k}$ finnally goes to $1$, because $\{k^{1/k}\} \to 1$, from which the average goes to $1$ by Cesaro-Stolz lemma.
Now replacing this sum by $\frac{1}{n} \sum^\infty_{k=1} n^{1/k}$, it helps to
estimate the new summation by splitting the sum into two pieces.

The summation is

$$n + n^{1/2} + n^{1/3} + \ldots n^{1/n}.$$

The first $\ln(n)$ terms can be estimated by summing $\sqrt n$.

Why would the upper bound $n^{1/k} \leq \sqrt n$ for the first $\ln(n)$ work?? The reason is that we know the sum
$\sum_{2 \leq k < \ln n} n^{1/k} \leq \ln(n) \sqrt n = o(n)$, and so this upper bound is sufficient.

Now we estimate $\sum_{\ln n \leq k \leq n} n^{1/k}$.

Inequality

The first inequality to use is

$$e^{\ln n /k} \leq \frac{\ln n}{k} + 1$$
for $k\geq \ln n$. ($e^x < 3 \implies e^x < 3x +1$ for $x\in [0,1]$)

Also, for $k \geq 2$,

$$1/k = \int^{k}_{k-1} \frac{1}{k} dt <\int^{k}_{k-1} \frac{1}{t} dt$$

So

$$\sum^n_{k=2} 1/k < \sum^n_{k=2} \int^k_{k-1} \frac{1}{t}dt = \int^n_{1} \frac{1}{t}dt =\ln n \tag{1}$$

Concluding Estimate

$$\sum_{\ln n < k \leq n} n^{1/k} = \sum_{\ln n < k \leq n} e^{\ln n/k} < 3 \ln n \left(\sum^n_{k=2} \frac{1}{k}\right) + n< 3\ln n \ln n + n = o(n) + n$$

entry.content:
1. Is
    $$\frac{1}{1 + z^n}$$
    convergent or divergent for complex number $z$?

Hints. Comparison test for positive series: Suppose $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ are positive series. If $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = A (\neq 0)$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ simutaneously convergent or divergent.
Term Test: If $\sum a_n$ is convergent, then $\lim_{n\to \infty}a_n =0$.

Solution. If $|z|<1$, then $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + z^n} = 1 \neq 0$. So the series $\sum \frac{1}{1 + z^n}$ diverge. If $|z|=1$, then

$$\left|\frac{1}{1 + z^n}\right| \geq \frac{1}{|1| + |z^n|} = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}.$$
from which $\sum \frac{1}{1 + z^n}$ diverge when $|z| = 1$. If $|z| >1$, then $\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{z^n}} = 1$. Let $b_n = \frac{1}{z^n}$. The series $\sum \frac{1}{1 + z^n}$ converges because
$$\lim \bigg(\frac{1}{1 + z^n}\bigg) \bigg/b_n = \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{z^n}} = 1$$
from which the comparison test confirms the convergence. $\square$

Let $e_1 = 1,\, e_2=x,\, e_3=x^2$. The invariant subspaces wrt $\Delta$ of $V$ are
$W_1={\rm span}(e_1), W_2={\rm span}(e_1, e_2), W_3= {\rm span}(e_1, e_2, e_3)$

Proof. Let $W$ be an invariant space of $W$ wrt $\Delta$.
Suppose $W_j$ is the maximal subspace in $\{W_k\}_{k=1,2,3}$ that contains $W$. Then we can show that $W$ contains $W_j$ as well. So $W=W_j$.
